meta.note: Every event has an evidence quote that is checked word-for-word against a primary source by data/scripts/check_timeline.py. Death numbers are checked against the CDC data file.

events.title: The Second Amendment is ratified
events.text: The states approve the Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments to the Constitution. The Second Amendment says: "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed."
events.why: For more than 200 years, people have argued about what this single sentence means. Supreme Court cases today still ask how gun laws compare with laws from this time.

sources.label: National Archives: Bill of Rights transcript
sources.quote: Ten of the proposed 12 amendments were ratified by three-fourths of the state legislatures on December 15, 1791.

events.title: National Firearms Act
events.text: Congress passes a federal gun law that puts strict controls on machine guns and defines what counts as a "machinegun".
events.why: This definition is still used today. In 2024, the Supreme Court case about bump stocks turned on the exact words written in 1934.

link.label: You be the judge: Garland v. Cargill

sources.label: Garland v. Cargill (2024), dissent
sources.quote: Congress has sharply restricted civilian ownership of machineguns since 1934.

events.title: United States v. Miller
events.text: The Supreme Court decides an early case about the Second Amendment and a federal gun law.
events.why: In 2008, the Court explained in Heller how it reads Miller: the case is about which kinds of weapons are protected, not about whether only militia members are protected.

sources.label: District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), syllabus
sources.quote: does not limit the right to keep and bear arms to militia purposes, but rather limits the type of weapon to which the right applies to those used by the militia

events.title: Gun Control Act
events.text: Congress creates a list of people who may not have guns under federal law, for example people convicted of serious crimes and fugitives from justice.
events.why: Two recent Supreme Court cases, Rahimi (2024) and Hemani (2026), were about people on this list.

link.label: You be the judge: United States v. Hemani

sources.label: United States v. Hemani (2026)
sources.quote: The federal Gun Control Act prohibits various categories of people from possessing guns.

events.title: Firearms Owners' Protection Act
events.text: Congress eases some federal rules for gun owners. The same law bans civilians from getting new machine guns. Machine guns that were already legally owned are still allowed.
events.why: It shows that one law can loosen some rules and tighten others at the same time.

sources.label: Public Law 99-308 (Statutes at Large)
sources.quote: it shall be unlawful for any person to transfer or possess a machinegun

sources.label: Public Law 99-308, approval date
sources.quote: Approved May 19, 1986.

events.title: Brady Act: background checks begin
events.text: Under the Brady Act, licensed gun dealers must check buyers' backgrounds. At first, there is also a five-day waiting period for handguns. In 1998, it is replaced by a national instant background check system (NICS).
events.why: Federal background checks apply only to licensed dealers. Sales between private people are left to the states, which is one reason state laws differ so much.

sources.label: RAND State Firearm Law Database, methods
sources.quote: in effect from February 28, 1994, to November 30, 1998

sources.label: RAND State Firearm Law Database, methods
sources.quote: 1998 (National Instant Criminal Background Check System)

events.title: Federal assault weapons ban (10 years)
events.text: A federal law bans the making, sale and possession of certain semiautomatic weapons, and of magazines that hold more than ten rounds. It applies only to weapons made after the ban began. The ban ends on September 13, 2004.
events.why: Since then, bans like this exist only in some states. In December 2026, the Supreme Court will hear a case about whether state bans on AR-15-style rifles are allowed.

sources.label: RAND State Firearm Law Database, methods
sources.quote: from September 13, 1994, to September 13, 2004

sources.label: RAND State Firearm Law Database, methods
sources.quote: magazines that hold more than ten rounds of ammunition

events.title: District of Columbia v. Heller
events.text: The Supreme Court rules 5 to 4 that the Second Amendment protects an individual's right to have a handgun at home for self-defense.
events.why: The Court said the right belongs to individual people, not only to members of a militia.

sources.label: District of Columbia v. Heller (2008)
sources.quote: Argued March 18, 2008—Decided June 26, 2008

events.title: McDonald v. Chicago
events.text: The Supreme Court rules that the Second Amendment limits state and local governments too, not only the federal government.
events.why: Before this, it was unclear whether states had to respect the right described in Heller. After McDonald, state gun laws can be challenged under the Second Amendment.

sources.label: Wolford v. Lopez (2026), syllabus
sources.quote: The Court later held in McDonald v. Chicago, 561 U. S. 742, that the Second Amendment right applies equally to the Federal

sources.label: United States v. Rahimi (2024)
sources.quote: McDonald v. Chicago, 561 U. S. 742, 778 (2010)

events.title: Las Vegas shooting
events.text: A shooter firing from a hotel room into an outdoor concert kills 58 people and wounds more than 500. He used rifles fitted with bump stocks.
events.why: After this shooting, the federal government changed its rules on bump stocks, which led to a Supreme Court case in 2024.

sources.label: Garland v. Cargill (2024), dissent
sources.quote: On October 1, 2017, a shooter opened fire from a hotel room overlooking an outdoor concert in Las Vegas, Nevada

sources.label: Garland v. Cargill (2024), dissent
sources.quote: the shooter killed 58 people and wounded over 500

events.title: Federal rule treats bump stocks as machine guns
events.text: The federal agency ATF issues a rule saying bump stocks count as machine guns under the 1934 law. Owners must destroy them or hand them in.
events.why: In 2024, the Supreme Court decided that the agency had gone beyond what the law's words allow.

link.label: You be the judge: Garland v. Cargill

sources.label: Garland v. Cargill (2024)
sources.quote: ATF issued its final Rule in 2018.

events.title: Gun deaths jump
events.text: Gun deaths rise from 39,707 in 2019 to 45,222 in 2020, the biggest one-year increase in the years shown on this site.
events.why: On its own, this data cannot tell us why deaths rose.

link.label: See the trend on the map

events.title: Gun deaths reach a peak
events.text: 48,830 people die from gun injuries, the highest number in the years covered on this site.
events.why: After 2021, the number goes down three years in a row, but it stays above every year from 2014 to 2019.

events.title: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen
events.text: The Supreme Court rules 6 to 3 that states may not require people to prove a special need before they can carry a handgun in public. It also creates a new test: gun laws must fit the nation's historical tradition.
events.why: This history test changed how courts judge gun laws. The Court used it again in Rahimi (2024), Hemani (2026) and Wolford (2026).

sources.label: NYSRPA v. Bruen (2022)
sources.quote: Argued November 3, 2021—Decided June 23, 2022

events.title: Bipartisan Safer Communities Act
events.text: Congress passes a federal gun law that makes straw purchasing (buying a gun for someone who is not allowed to have one) and gun trafficking specific federal crimes. It extends the domestic-violence gun ban to dating partners, and gives states money for crisis programs, including red flag programs.
events.why: It became law two days after the Bruen decision.

sources.label: Public Law 117-159
sources.quote: Approved June 25, 2022.

sources.label: Public Law 117-159
sources.quote: section 932 (relating to straw purchasing), section 933 (relating to trafficking in firearms)

sources.label: Public Law 117-159
sources.quote: or by a person who has a current or recent former dating relationship with the victim

sources.label: Public Law 117-159
sources.quote: extreme risk protection order programs

events.title: Garland v. Cargill
events.text: The Supreme Court rules 6 to 3 that a rifle with a bump stock is not a "machinegun" under the 1934 law, so the 2018 rule is invalid.
events.why: The case was about the meaning of a law's words, not the Constitution. Congress can change the law if it wants to.

sources.label: Garland v. Cargill (2024)
sources.quote: Argued February 28, 2024—Decided June 14, 2024

events.title: United States v. Rahimi
events.text: The Supreme Court rules 8 to 1 that a person whom a court has found to be a credible threat to someone else's safety can be temporarily disarmed.
events.why: It explained that modern gun laws do not need an exact "historical twin" to pass the Bruen test.

sources.label: United States v. Rahimi (2024)
sources.quote: Argued November 7, 2023—Decided June 21, 2024

events.title: 44,447 gun deaths
events.text: Gun deaths fall for the third year in a row, to 44,447. That is still more than in any year from 2014 to 2019.
events.why: These are the latest final numbers from CDC used on this site.

events.title: United States v. Hemani
events.text: All nine justices agree that a man could not be prosecuted for having a gun at home only because he regularly used marijuana.
events.why: The Court called its decision narrow. It shows that the federal list of people who may not have guns can be challenged, one situation at a time.

sources.label: United States v. Hemani (2026)
sources.quote: Argued March 2, 2026—Decided June 18, 2026

events.title: Wolford v. Lopez
events.text: The Supreme Court rules 6 to 3 against a Hawaii law that banned permit holders from carrying guns onto private property open to the public (like stores or gas stations) unless the owner clearly allowed it.
events.why: Owners can still say no to guns on their property. The Court ruled against making a ban on guns the automatic rule when the owner has said nothing.

sources.label: Wolford v. Lopez (2026)
sources.quote: Argued January 20, 2026—Decided June 25, 2026

sources.label: Wolford v. Lopez (2026), syllabus
sources.quote: owners of establishments that are open to the public can admit or exclude persons who are carrying guns for self-defense

sources.quote: Kagan, J., filed a dissenting opinion. Jackson, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Sotomayor, J., joined.

events.title: Coming up: Can states ban AR-15-style rifles?
events.text: The Supreme Court will hear two cases together, Viramontes v. Cook County and Grant v. Higgins. The question: "Whether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee the right to possess AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles." The decision has not been made yet.
events.why: The answer could affect state laws that ban these rifles. Nobody, including us, knows the outcome yet.

sources.quote: Whether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee the right to possess AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles.
